Where the assembly met is not stated, and the guesses differ with the reasoning behind them. Henry canvasses Timnath-serah, on the ground that Joshua was too old to travel, and rejects it because it does not appear he took so much state upon him; he prefers Shiloh, where the tabernacle was, and supposes the occasion was one of the three great feasts when the men had come up anyway. Wesley reaches Shiloh by a different route, that words uttered before the Lord were likely to have more effect. Gill leaves all three possibilities open, Timnath-serah, Shechem and Shiloh, and observes that all Israel cannot mean the whole body unless a feast had gathered them, so this was an occasional convocation of representatives rather than a stated one. Clarke does not decide the place either, but insists on a point the others pass over, that this assembly and the one at Shechem in the next chapter are two distinct meetings and not one. Keil sets the scene differently again, with Joshua already withdrawn to Timnath-serah to enjoy his own inheritance in quiet, and drawn out of it by the remembrance of the charge once given him.

On the timing Clarke is most precise, placing this in the hundred and tenth and last year of Joshua's life, thirteen or fourteen years after the conquest and seven after the division; Wesley says simply about fourteen years. Henry declines a figure and gives instead two reasons why the interval mattered: long enough for Israel to feel the comfort of their rest and enjoy the good land, and long enough for Joshua to observe which way their danger lay, namely their intimacy with the Canaanites who remained. Ellicott finds the phrase about age worth pausing on, since the same words were used of Joshua years earlier, and offers the figure of the two evenings of his life, the early one when his sun began to decline and the late one just before its setting, remarking that Israel received their inheritance between them. Henry and Wesley both take the old man's age as itself an argument. He would not be long preaching to them, so what he said should be laid up for the time to come; and Henry adds that having grown old in their service he was the more to be regarded, since days should speak. Clarke identifies the four ranks summoned, elders, heads of families, judges who decided causes and officers who executed the sentences.

Why any Canaanites were left at all draws three incompatible answers. Ellicott takes the arrangement as deliberate and provisional: here and elsewhere the preliminary and partial nature of the conquest is distinctly recognised, Joshua having given Israel the land to possess and the vantage-ground from which to possess it, and now bidding them continue the work he began. Clarke attributes the survival to Israel instead, saying the old inhabitants held many districts more through the supineness of the Israelites than through any bravery of their own, the Canaanite armies having long been broken. Calvin says the same more sharply and turns it into a lesson about gratitude: it was owing to their cowardice that they dwelt among enemies whom it would not have been difficult to rout, and the peace they enjoyed is nonetheless credited as an excellent blessing, so that thanks are due to God for pardoning their ingratitude. Clarke also catches the modesty of the speech, that Israel would naturally have credited their veteran general with the conquest, and that Joshua corrects them by insisting the battle was the Lord's. Gill and Keil keep to the promise that the remainder would yet be expelled, and Clarke notes that one Hebrew word serves both for disinheriting them and for inheriting their land.

On what the courage is for, the answers pull in different directions. Wesley makes it practical, since great resolution was needed to execute all the commands of Moses and particularly to expel the residue of the Canaanites, and he glosses turning aside as adding to the law or diminishing from it. Clarke moves it inward, that it takes no small courage to keep a sound creed among scoffers and no less to maintain a godly practice among the profane, and adds that God's people are bound by his word alone, nothing being received as an article of faith which God has not spoken. Ellicott sees the office rather than the effort: Joshua was himself the servant of the law and his successors must be the same, no higher position being attainable, and nothing has ever superseded the authority of the written word. Calvin explains why the word is strong at all: in the great weakness of our nature no man will set about a thorough observance of the Law unless he exerts himself above his strength, and the command warns against substituting gross security for genuine confidence, since hypocrites boast of the promises while true faith keeps a man in fear.

The prohibition on so much as naming their gods is read as a study in gradual corruption. Wesley takes the point to be that mention breeds discourse, and discourse by insensible steps brings approbation and then worship, so that things not evil in themselves may be forbidden as introductions to evil; he adds the complaint that among Christians the names of the heathen gods are still so commonly used, especially in poems. Clarke traces the same descent as a chain, from civil contracts to spiritual affinities, then to honourable mention, swearing, serving and bowing, reinforcing it with the maxim that no man reaches the worst by a single step and the note that even Nero was once a promising youth. Keil classifies rather than warns, treating the naming, the swearing, the serving and the bowing as the four outward forms of divine worship. Calvin notes what is absent from the list, that neither bending the knee nor sacrifices are specified, so that all perverse worship is designated at once, and infers that God is defrauded of his honour whenever any particle of what he claims is transferred to an idol.

The promise that one shall chase a thousand divides the commentators over its tense. Gill reports that two Jewish expositors take the future for the past, so that the saying records what had already happened in the war, and that a third disapproves and refers it forward to what they would do if they clave to the Lord, as afterwards in Samson. Clarke reads it as a spur against inaction, that they need not wait to become more numerous before driving out their enemies. Wesley reads it as a caution the other way, that they must not impute past victories to their own valour, as they would be apt to do. Gill fills in what made the enemy formidable: populous nations of able-bodied men, some of gigantic stature, in fortified cities with chariots of iron. On the closing charge to love God, Clarke notes that the Hebrew rendered soul covers the whole self, so body and soul are both engaged; Henry turns it into two rules: we must stand upon our guard, since many a precious soul is ruined through carelessness, and what we do in religion must proceed from love and not from slavish fear. Calvin makes that the root of everything: without free and ardent affection we study in vain to frame our lives by the outward form of the Law. Wesley warns that watchfulness is harder now than in the wilderness, the temptations being stronger from bad neighbours and from prosperity.

Clarke reads the warning in military terms first, that a soldier who draws back on going to meet the enemy forfeits his life, and these were the Lord's soldiers. He then takes the figures separately: a net set by the fowler for heedless birds, a trap laid to catch the unwary traveller by the foot, and the two that admit no relief, a goad in the side and a thorn in the eye. His application is that the surviving nations would drive Israel into the service of false gods and put out the eyes of their understanding, and that God would preserve them for exactly that purpose. Wesley adds the sequence by which it happens, converse leading by degrees into their errors and lusts, and then presses what the end would feel like: they would be forced to quit their own land and wander they knew not where, which must have been terrible to men comparing their present ease and plenty with the hazards and wants of their former wandering. Calvin explains why threatening is used at all, that those not allured by God's goodness may be aroused by fear, since such is the lethargy of the flesh that it always requires stimulating.

On Joshua's announcement of his own death the commentators are unusually close in phrase. Gill calls death a journey from this world to another, a going to one's long home, a path trodden by all men and but once, from which none is exempted, be he ever so great or good or useful; Wesley says almost the same in almost the same words, that to die is to go a journey to our long home, and that Joshua, ill as he could be spared, was not exempted from the common lot. Both add that he says it so they will take these for his dying words. Calvin reads the sentence as consolation rather than as a claim on their attention: the loss would leave the people as a mutilated trunk deprived of its head, so Joshua tells them not to ask that his condition should differ from the whole human race. He is careful to qualify it, noting that the form of dying is not the same in all, since those who receive the heavenly doctrine are distinguished by an incorruptible seed, and that only what is common to all is in view here. Keil takes the phrase about knowing in all their hearts and souls to mean that they were fully convinced.

The argument turns on a symmetry, and Clarke and Wesley state it identically: God's faithfulness in fulfilling his promises is the proof that he will as faithfully accomplish his threatenings, since his veracity is equally pledged for both. Ellicott makes the claim carry historical weight, observing that though the conquest was in one sense limited, the declaration that nothing had failed shows it satisfied Israel's hopes for the time, so they understood the promises in the sense in which they were fulfilled. Ellicott also identifies who the address was aimed at, since the matters raised in it lie within the province of the ruler: marriages, treaties and public worship are under the control of law, and what the magistrates will not enforce the people will find it hard to maintain. Clarke reports another writer's remark that the speech follows the rhetorician's rule, milder affections at the beginning and piercing passages toward the end, and adds his verdict that no people were ever more fairly warned and none profited less. Keil and Gill supply the covenantal frame, the evil word being the curse of rejection already spoken through Moses. Wesley closes on a quarrel of his own, quoting an earlier English expositor on how the goodness of the heavenly Canaan will aggravate the misery of those shut out from it, and then turning that very sentence against the doctrine of absolute decrees.
